clips.text: Welcome. This lesson follows the website, not the order of an audiobook. We will explore the heart as a pump, trace its electrical signal, zoom into muscle contraction, and connect the lungs to circulation. Then we will use those ideas to understand E C G recordings. Each short section has a matching transcript. Pause, replay, or explore before continuing. The later rhythm and pacemaker chapters are separate study modules.

Begin with the whole system. Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs work together in systems. Homeostasis means maintaining a relatively stable internal environment. The lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide with the air. The heart creates pressure that moves blood. Blood vessels distribute that blood, and tissues exchange gases and nutrients across capillaries. Oxygen delivery depends on all of these parts, not on one monitor number alone.

Before we name a structure, establish the patient's directions. Right and left always mean the patient's right and left. Anterior means toward the front; posterior, toward the back. Superior means toward the head; inferior, toward the feet. Medial is toward the midline; lateral is away from it. A frontal plane separates front from back. A transverse plane separates upper from lower regions. A sagittal plane separates left from right.

Locate the heart behind the sternum, between the lungs, in the mediastinum. Its apex points down and toward the patient's left. The adult heart is roughly the size of that person's fist, but size varies. The rib cage normally has twelve pairs of ribs. The spaces between adjacent ribs are intercostal spaces. These chest landmarks will matter again when we place recording electrodes.

Add four pairs of location words. Proximal means closer to a point of attachment; distal means farther from it. The wrist is distal to the elbow. Superficial means nearer the body surface; deep means farther inside. Cranial and caudal roughly indicate toward the head and toward the lower end of the trunk. Ventral and dorsal usually correspond to anterior and posterior in the human trunk. Apply each term to a named structure rather than memorizing an isolated definition.

Check your orientation. In a front view of the patient, is the patient's right side on your right or your left? Pause and point to it. Then identify the sternum and the space occupied by the heart. Continue when you can explain why patient-centered directions prevent mistakes when locating chest electrodes.

Find the four chambers in the heart. The right atrium and left atrium receive returning blood. The right ventricle and left ventricle eject blood. The septum separates the right and left sides. Now trace the two connected routes. Blood returning from the body enters the right atrium, passes into the right ventricle, and travels to the lungs. Blood returning from the lungs enters the left atrium, passes into the left ventricle, and leaves for the body. Both sides pump during the same heartbeat, but toward different destinations. The right side supplies the pulmonary circuit. The left side supplies the systemic circuit. Pause here and point to each chamber. Use the patient's right and left, even when the front view reverses them on your screen.

Start the blood-flow journey at the right atrium. The superior vena cava returns blood from much of the upper body. The inferior vena cava returns blood from much of the lower body. The coronary sinus returns much of the blood that has supplied the heart muscle itself. This returning blood contains less oxygen than blood leaving the lungs, but it is not completely without oxygen.

clips.text: Follow blood from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. Tricuspid means three cusps. This is an atrioventricular valve, because it lies between an atrium and a ventricle. When ventricular pressure rises, the valve closes and limits backward flow into the atrium. Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles help keep the valve cusps from prolapsing backward during contraction; they do not pull the valve open.
clips.running_balance_note: Arithmetic reconstruction from each UI-verified charge; intermediate live displays may lag.

clips.text: The right ventricle ejects blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, which branches toward the two lungs. The pulmonary valve is a semilunar valve. Its pocket-like cusps limit backward flow into the ventricle after ejection. Arteries are named for carrying blood away from the heart, not for carrying oxygen-rich blood. The pulmonary arteries are the important example: they carry relatively oxygen-poor blood toward the lungs.
clips.running_balance_note: Arithmetic reconstruction from each UI-verified charge; intermediate live displays may lag.

clips.text: In the pulmonary capillaries, blood comes close to air inside the alveoli without normally mixing with that air. Oxygen moves into the blood, and carbon dioxide moves toward the alveolar air. The pulmonary veins then return relatively oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium. Usually four pulmonary veins enter the left atrium. A vein carries blood toward the heart, so pulmonary veins remain veins even though their blood is oxygen-rich.

clips.text: Blood passes from the left atrium through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. The mitral valve is also called the bicuspid valve because it normally has two cusps. Notice the thicker muscular wall of the left ventricle. It must generate the pressure needed for systemic circulation. Compare wall thickness, not a claim that the left ventricular chamber is always larger. In a steady state, both ventricles pump approximately the same volume per minute.

clips.text: The left ventricle ejects blood through the aortic valve into the aorta. From there, arteries branch into smaller arteries and arterioles. Capillary networks bring blood close to tissue cells. After exchange, blood enters venules and veins, eventually returning to the right atrium. The aortic valve is the second semilunar valve. Like the other valves, it opens and closes in response to pressure differences across it.

clips.text: The pulmonary and systemic circuits are connected in series. Pulmonary circulation runs from the right ventricle through the lungs to the left atrium. Systemic circulation runs from the left ventricle through the body to the right atrium. The heart's own coronary circulation is part of the systemic circuit. Blood-flow arrows should always follow this route. Red and blue are teaching colors for relative oxygen content; human blood is never actually blue.
clips.running_balance_note: Arithmetic reconstruction from each UI-verified charge; intermediate live displays may lag.

clips.text: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it toward the heart. Arterioles regulate resistance and distribute flow. Capillaries are thin exchange vessels. Larger vessels have an inner tunica intima, a middle tunica media, and an outer tunica externa. The lumen is the open space inside. Vasoconstriction narrows the lumen; vasodilation widens it. Many veins have valves that help limit backward flow, especially in the limbs.

clips.text: Blood contains plasma and formed elements. Plasma is the liquid transport medium. Red blood cells contain hemoglobin, which carries most blood oxygen. White blood cells participate in immune defense. Platelets help form clots. Carbon dioxide travels in several forms, especially as bicarbonate in plasma. Tissue perfusion means blood flowing through tissues; adequate oxygen delivery also depends on the amount of hemoglobin, its oxygen saturation, and the flow reaching those tissues.

clips.text: The heart muscle needs its own blood supply. Coronary arteries branch from the aorta. Major vessels include the right coronary artery and the left coronary artery, which gives rise to the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries. Cardiac veins return much of this blood through the coronary sinus. Left ventricular coronary flow is greatest during diastole, largely because contraction compresses vessels in the ventricular wall. Valve closure is not a switch that turns coronary flow on.

clips.text: Now trace a complete circuit yourself. Begin at the right atrium. Name each valve and chamber, visit the lungs, return to the left side, and leave through the aorta. Then explain two exceptions to the shortcut that arteries contain oxygen-rich blood and veins contain oxygen-poor blood. Use the actual definitions: away from the heart for arteries, toward the heart for veins.

clips.text: Separate the heart wall from the sac around it. The heart wall has three layers: epicardium outside, myocardium in the middle, and endocardium inside. The myocardium provides most of the pumping force. The endocardium lines the chambers and covers the valves. The pericardium surrounds the heart. Its serous layers and small amount of fluid reduce friction. The visceral layer of serous pericardium is also the epicardium.

Most cardiomyocytes are working contractile cells; specialized cardiomyocytes initiate and conduct impulses. They are striated, branched cells connected at intercalated discs. Mechanical junctions help cells remain attached during contraction. Gap junctions allow electrical current to pass between neighboring cells. Together, these connections help groups of cells activate and contract in a coordinated way. The heart has intrinsic electrical activity; nerves adjust its behavior rather than commanding every individual heartbeat.

Watch ventricular filling. When ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, the atrioventricular valves open and blood enters the ventricles. Much filling is passive. The slower middle portion of filling is called diastasis. Near the end of ventricular diastole, atrial contraction adds more blood. This contribution is sometimes called the atrial kick. Its size varies with heart rate, age, and ventricular stiffness, so it is not a fixed percentage for every person or every beat.

Next, the ventricles begin to contract. Rising pressure closes the atrioventricular valves. For a brief period, the semilunar valves have not opened yet, so all four valves are closed. Pressure rises while ventricular volume changes very little. This is isovolumetric contraction. The papillary muscles also contract, supporting the closed atrioventricular valves. Remember the sequence: electrical activation starts first; force and pressure develop afterward.

When ventricular pressure exceeds pressure in the pulmonary trunk and aorta, the semilunar valves open. Blood is ejected into the pulmonary and systemic circuits. The atrioventricular valves remain closed during this phase. The two ventricles work against different pressures, but they normally eject similar stroke volumes over time. The heart does not empty completely with each beat; some blood remains in each ventricle after ejection.

As ventricular muscle relaxes, pressure falls and the semilunar valves close. During isovolumetric relaxation, all valves are briefly closed again. Once ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, the atrioventricular valves reopen and filling resumes. Systole refers to contraction; diastole to relaxation and filling. These terms describe mechanical events. An E C G is an electrical recording, so its waves are related to, but not identical with, these phases.

Heart rate is beats per minute. Stroke volume is the volume ejected by one ventricle per beat. Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume. For example, seventy beats per minute times seventy milliliters per beat equals four thousand nine hundred milliliters per minute, or four point nine liters per minute. A resting adult output around four to eight liters per minute is a broad teaching reference, not a result predicted from an E C G alone.

Stroke volume depends partly on preload, afterload, and contractility. Preload relates to ventricular filling and muscle stretch before contraction. Afterload is the load the ventricle must overcome to eject blood. Contractility is the muscle's intrinsic ability to develop force. Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume. A commonly used left ventricular reference range is about fifty-five to seventy percent. It is not the percentage of all blood in the body pumped per beat.

Check the pump before moving to electricity. Which valves are open during ventricular ejection? Which are open during most ventricular filling? What happens to cardiac output if rate changes but stroke volume also changes? Blood pressure reflects interactions among cardiac output, vascular resistance, and other factors. A normal-looking rhythm does not prove normal pressure, normal ejection fraction, or adequate tissue perfusion.

Now keep the same anatomical heart and follow its electrical pathway. Specialized cells initiate and conduct impulses, and working muscle cells produce force. Automaticity is spontaneous impulse generation. Excitability is responding to a stimulus. Conductivity is transmitting electrical activity. Contractility is developing force. These properties are related but not interchangeable. Electrical activation organizes the sequence of contraction; it does not by itself prove that the heart is pumping effectively.

Find the sinoatrial node, or S A node, high in the right atrium near the superior vena cava. It is normally the dominant pacemaker. Its cells depolarize spontaneously, and activity spreads through the atrial muscle. A usual resting adult sinus rate is sixty to one hundred beats per minute. This is a clinical teaching range, not a claim that every healthy person's resting rate must fall inside it.

The impulse spreads across both atria and reaches the atrioventricular node, or A V node. Conduction slows substantially here. This delay helps coordinate atrial activation with ventricular activation, giving the ventricles time to fill before they contract. Do not spread this delay evenly along the whole pathway. After the A V node, the specialized ventricular conduction system is designed for rapid conduction.

From the A V node, the impulse enters the bundle of His, then the right and left bundle branches in the interventricular septum. Purkinje fibers rapidly distribute activation through the ventricles. This organization helps the ventricular muscle activate efficiently, with contraction developing from the apex toward the outflow regions. The colors in the overlay represent the teaching sequence, not the physical color of electricity inside the heart.

If the normal dominant pacemaker slows or impulses fail to reach lower tissue, an escape pacemaker may emerge. Usual teaching ranges are forty to sixty beats per minute for junctional escape and twenty to forty for ventricular escape. These are approximate ranges. Conduction speed and firing rate are different ideas: the A V node conducts slowly, while Purkinje tissue conducts rapidly. The fastest focus does not always control the heart if conduction is blocked.

Zoom conceptually from the heart to one ventricular muscle cell. Its action potential begins with rapid sodium entry. A brief early change is followed by a plateau, during which calcium entry and potassium exit both matter. Potassium currents then help repolarize the cell. These changing currents flow through ion channels. The sodium-potassium pump maintains ion gradients over time; it is not the channel that produces every action-potential upstroke.

Pacemaker cells do not have the same stable resting potential or the same action-potential shape as ventricular working cells. Their membrane voltage drifts toward threshold, and calcium current contributes to the nodal upstroke. Threshold and resting values vary by cell type and conditions. Do not label calcium, sodium, and potassium with voltages as if those were their electrical charges. An ion's charge and its equilibrium potential are different quantities.

Now connect electricity to force. Calcium entering a cardiac muscle cell triggers a larger calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, the cell's internal calcium store. Calcium binds to troponin. This moves tropomyosin away from actin's binding sites so myosin can interact with actin. The process is called excitation-contraction coupling. The electrical signal starts the sequence, but calcium handling and the contractile machinery determine how force develops.

Within a muscle cell, myofibrils contain repeating sarcomeres. Each sarcomere spans from one Z line to the next. At the sarcomere, myosin heads bind to actin, produce force, detach, and reset through repeated cross-bridge cycles. A T P is needed for this cycle, including detachment of myosin from actin. Thin and thick filaments slide past one another; the filaments themselves do not become shorter. The distance between the sarcomere boundaries decreases. Many sarcomeres acting together shorten the muscle cell and contribute to ventricular pressure.

For relaxation, the free calcium concentration in the cell must fall. Much calcium returns to the sarcoplasmic reticulum through an A T P-dependent pump. Calcium also leaves the cell, especially through the sodium-calcium exchanger. As calcium dissociates from troponin, tropomyosin again limits actin-myosin interaction. The sodium-potassium pump supports the gradients that make this system possible. Relaxation is an active, energy-dependent process, not simply the absence of an electrical wave.

Ions are atoms or molecules carrying an electrical charge. Sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium are positive ions; chloride is a negative ion. Different concentrations inside and outside the cell, together with selective membrane permeability, create electrical and chemical gradients. The sodium-potassium pump uses A T P to move three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in. This maintains gradients over time and indirectly supports calcium handling; channels carry the rapid currents of each action potential.

During the refractory period, cardiac muscle cannot respond normally to another stimulus. Early in recovery, a new propagated response cannot be triggered normally; later, a sufficiently strong premature stimulus may trigger one. These cellular periods do not have one exact boundary on every surface T wave. Put the sequence in order: impulse spread, calcium release, cross-bridge force, calcium removal, and relaxation. Then return to the original heart and trace S A node to Purkinje fibers.

Trace the air pathway. Air enters through the nose or mouth. The nasal cavity filters, warms, and humidifies air. The pharynx has named regions: the nasopharynx behind the nasal cavity, the oropharynx behind the oral cavity, and the laryngopharynx farther down. These regions are not simply alternate names for the nose and mouth. The airway shares part of its route with the digestive pathway before the routes separate.

The larynx contains the vocal folds and connects the pharynx to the trachea. During swallowing, coordinated movements protect the airway; the epiglottis helps cover the laryngeal opening. The trachea then carries air toward the lungs. Definitions of the upper-lower airway boundary differ among courses, so this lesson will name the actual structures rather than make the boundary itself a physiological rule.

The trachea divides into the right and left main bronchi. Inside the lungs, branches become smaller bronchi and bronchioles. The right lung normally has three lobes, and the left has two. The conducting airways transport air. Farther along, the respiratory zone includes respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, and alveoli. Follow the route rather than treating the pleura or diaphragm as structures that air passes through.

Terminal bronchioles are the final part of the conducting zone. They do not contain the alveoli needed for ordinary gas exchange. Respiratory bronchioles, which come after them, have alveoli in their walls and begin the respiratory zone. Anatomical dead space is air in conducting passages that does not participate in gas exchange. Physiological dead space also includes ventilated alveoli that receive too little blood flow for effective exchange.

The visceral pleura covers the lung surface. The parietal pleura lines the inside of the thoracic wall. A thin fluid layer between them reduces friction and helps the lungs follow movements of the chest wall. This is normally a potential space, not a large air-filled gap. Air or excess fluid entering the pleural space can interfere with expansion. Keep the pleura separate from the branching airway route.

Watch inspiration. The diaphragm contracts and moves downward, becoming flatter. External intercostal muscles help lift and expand the rib cage. Thoracic volume increases, the lungs expand, and alveolar pressure briefly falls below atmospheric pressure. Air moves inward down that pressure gradient. The diaphragm does not pull air directly through a tube; its movement changes the dimensions and pressure relationships of the thorax.

During quiet expiration, the diaphragm relaxes and the elastic recoil of the respiratory system helps reduce lung volume. Alveolar pressure briefly rises above atmospheric pressure, and air moves out. Quiet expiration is usually passive. Forced breathing can recruit additional muscles, including abdominal and accessory inspiratory muscles. One breath contains an inspiratory phase and an expiratory phase; count a complete cycle, not each movement as a separate breath.

At the alveolus, a very thin barrier separates air from pulmonary capillary blood. Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into blood because its partial pressure is higher in the alveolus. Carbon dioxide diffuses in the opposite direction because its partial pressure is higher in the arriving blood. Diffusion itself is passive. A large surface area, a thin barrier, ventilation, and blood flow all support effective exchange.

Ventilation means moving air into and out of the lungs. Perfusion means blood flow through tissue, including pulmonary capillaries. External respiration is gas exchange between alveoli and blood. Internal respiration is exchange between systemic blood and tissues. Cellular respiration is the chemical process by which cells use energy substrates, often consuming oxygen and producing carbon dioxide. These ideas connect, but they are not interchangeable names for the same event.

Carbon dioxide participates in the bicarbonate buffer system. If other factors remain similar, retaining more carbon dioxide tends to lower blood pH, while removing more tends to raise it. Arterial blood pH is normally tightly regulated around seven point three five to seven point four five. The lungs and kidneys both contribute to acid-base regulation. A visible chest rise alone does not tell us whether ventilation is removing carbon dioxide adequately.

Networks in the medulla and pons generate and shape the breathing pattern. Central chemoreceptors respond mainly to changes related to carbon dioxide and cerebrospinal-fluid pH. Peripheral chemoreceptors also respond to oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH. Sensory input through nerves, including the vagus, modifies the pattern. It is too simple to say that chemoreceptors alone initiate every breath or that the vagus always increases breathing rate.

Follow an oxygen molecule from the alveolus into pulmonary blood, through the left atrium and left ventricle, and into the systemic circulation. Then follow carbon dioxide in the opposite overall journey, from tissues back to the lungs. Before continuing, explain the difference between moving air and exchanging gas. Which muscle drives most quiet inspiration, and why do terminal bronchioles conduct air rather than exchange gases?

Respiratory rate counts breaths per minute. A commonly taught resting adult range is twelve to twenty, but age, activity, and clinical circumstances matter. Monitors may estimate breathing from changes in electrical impedance between chest electrodes. Such estimates can contain artifact or miss important problems. A displayed number is not the same as observing breathing depth, effort, pattern, and the person being monitored.

Pulse oximetry estimates the percentage of hemoglobin binding sites occupied by oxygen in pulsating arterial blood. The device compares absorption of red and infrared light. It does not directly measure total oxygen content, ventilation, or carbon dioxide. Think of saturation as the fraction of seats occupied on oxygen-carrying buses, not the number of buses available. That is why hemoglobin concentration and blood flow also matter for oxygen delivery.

Many healthy people at sea level have readings from ninety-five to one hundred percent. One hundred percent is not automatically abnormal, and a pulse-oximeter reading alone does not establish oxygen toxicity. Motion, poor perfusion, nail products, dyshemoglobins, and device limitations can affect results. Accuracy can also differ across skin pigmentation. Carbon monoxide exposure can produce misleading readings on ordinary pulse oximeters. Interpret the measurement in context, not as a stand-alone assurance.

Capnography displays carbon dioxide in exhaled gas over time. End-tidal carbon dioxide is the value near the end of exhalation. A common reference range in a healthy resting adult is thirty-five to forty-five millimeters of mercury, but the value depends on ventilation, perfusion, metabolism, and equipment. The waveform changes as exhaled gas moves from conducting-airway gas toward alveolar gas. It is not interchangeable with a direct arterial carbon dioxide measurement.

Match each tool to the question it helps answer. Respiratory rate describes frequency. Pulse oximetry estimates arterial oxygen saturation. Capnography reflects exhaled carbon dioxide and ventilation-related information. The E C G records electrical activity of the heart. None of these alone proves adequate perfusion or gives a complete assessment. This lesson teaches what the signals mean, not how to prescribe oxygen, perform resuscitation, or choose a treatment.

An electrode is the sensor contacting the skin. A cable connects it to the recording system. An E C G lead is a calculated view of the heart's electrical activity, not simply the wire. A standard twelve-lead E C G uses ten electrodes to create twelve views. Six are limb-lead views, and six are chest-lead views. Keep those counts separate before placing anything on the body.

Lead one compares the left arm with the right arm. Lead two compares the left leg with the right arm. Lead three compares the left leg with the left arm. The first location named is positive in each comparison. The remaining limb electrode does not become the ground for that lead. A separate right-leg electrode commonly provides a reference or driven-right-leg function in the recording system.

The augmented limb leads are a V R, a V L, and a V F. They view the heart from the right arm, left arm, and left leg, using calculated references. Together with leads one, two, and three, they show the frontal plane. Chest leads V one through V six view the heart in the transverse plane, each relative to a combined reference. The word unipolar is traditional shorthand; a voltage measurement still requires a comparison.

Use the patient's landmarks, not guessed distances. The sternal angle helps identify the second rib; the second intercostal space lies just below it. From there, count down. The midclavicular line descends from the midpoint of the clavicle. The anterior axillary line and midaxillary line descend from the front and middle of the armpit. There are twelve pairs of ribs and eleven intercostal spaces on each side.

Locate V one at the fourth intercostal space, right sternal border, and V two at the fourth intercostal space, left sternal border. Locate V four at the fifth intercostal space on the left midclavicular line. V three lies halfway between V two and V four. V five is at the left anterior axillary line and V six at the left midaxillary line, both horizontally level with V four. Practice only in the website's learning model.

Good recordings depend on reliable skin contact, secure electrodes, correct positions, and a relaxed, still subject. Movement, muscle activity, loose contacts, and electrical interference can distort a tracing. Limb-electrode colors vary by standard, so read the labels instead of relying on a color mnemonic alone. Torso placements used for continuous monitoring are not automatically equivalent to standard diagnostic limb placements. Follow the particular recording protocol rather than treating every configuration as interchangeable.

A lead records the projection of the heart's changing electrical activity onto that lead's axis. A depolarization wave moving toward its positive pole usually creates a positive deflection; moving away usually creates a negative one. A near-perpendicular net vector can produce a small or biphasic complex. An isoelectric segment does not prove that every heart cell is electrically inactive. Opposing signals or little net change can also produce a near-flat line.

The usual adult frontal Q R S axis reference is minus thirty to plus ninety degrees. Leads one and a V F give a quick quadrant screen. Both positive generally fits the normal quadrant. Lead one positive with a V F negative is not automatically left axis deviation: the axis may still lie between zero and minus thirty degrees. Lead two helps distinguish that borderline-normal region from a more leftward axis. Axis is a clue, not a diagnosis by itself.

Check calibration before measuring. At a paper speed of twenty-five millimeters per second, one small horizontal box represents zero point zero four seconds. One large box represents zero point two zero seconds. At the usual gain of ten millimeters per millivolt, one small vertical box represents zero point one millivolt. Different speed or gain changes these relationships. A whole cardiac cycle is not always zero point eight seconds; its duration changes with rate.

The P wave represents atrial depolarization. In a typical sinus rhythm in lead two, it is upright and similar from beat to beat. The P R interval runs from the beginning of the P wave to the beginning of the Q R S complex. A common adult reference is zero point one two to zero point two zero seconds. It includes atrial depolarization and conduction toward the ventricles, including the A V nodal delay. It is not the duration of that delay alone.

The Q R S complex represents ventricular depolarization. Measure from its beginning to its end, at the transition into the S T segment called the J point. A duration below zero point one two seconds is usually described as narrow in adult rhythm teaching. Not every complex contains a visible Q, R, and S wave. A wide complex can reflect ventricular origin, but also bundle-branch block, aberrant conduction, pre-excitation, pacing, or other causes.

The S T segment extends from the J point to the start of the T wave. The T wave represents ventricular repolarization. Atrial repolarization is usually obscured by the much larger Q R S complex. A U wave may follow the T wave, but is not always visible. S T elevation or depression can have several causes; a single teaching strip does not establish infarction or ischemia without the full clinical and lead context.

The Q T interval runs from the start of the Q R S complex to the end of the T wave. It spans ventricular depolarization and repolarization. Q T changes with heart rate, so interpretation often uses a corrected value, called Q T c. The half-R-R rule is only a rough screening shortcut, not a substitute for proper correction and context. Different correction formulas have limitations, especially at very fast or slow rates.

Use the same method on every strip. First, assess regularity. Second, calculate atrial and ventricular rates when possible. Third, examine P waves and their relationship to Q R S complexes. Fourth, measure P R intervals and look for patterns. Fifth, measure Q R S duration and compare shapes. Sixth, evaluate Q T where the strip permits it. Describe the evidence before choosing a rhythm name. Electrical rate does not necessarily equal an effective pulse rate.

Compare successive R to R intervals for ventricular regularity and P to P intervals for atrial regularity. Calipers or a marked strip can help. An early atrial, junctional, or ventricular beat may interrupt an otherwise regular rhythm. Describe the underlying rhythm and then the premature complex. Ectopic means originating outside the usual pacemaker site; not every ectopic event is premature, because escape beats arise late when higher pacing fails.

On a six-second strip, count Q R S complexes and multiply by ten for an estimated ventricular rate. For a regular rhythm at standard speed, divide three hundred by the number of large boxes between consecutive R waves, or fifteen hundred by the small-box count. Three large boxes equal fifteen small boxes, so both calculations give one hundred beats per minute. Eighteen small boxes give about eighty-three. Those are different intervals, not competing answers for the same spacing.

If a verified practice strip is available in the website, work through it now. Mark P waves, measure the P R interval, measure Q R S duration, and compare R to R spacing. If atrial activity is not visible, say so rather than inventing a P wave. Record what can and cannot be measured. A strip's label must come from the actual image and measurements; the audiobook's references to unseen numbered figures are not enough to recreate their answers.

In normal sinus rhythm, the S A node initiates the rhythm, each visible sinus P wave is followed by a Q R S complex, and the P R relationship is consistent. The usual adult teaching rate is sixty to one hundred beats per minute. In lead two, P waves are typically upright and uniform. A narrow Q R S supports usual ventricular conduction. These electrical features do not guarantee normal cardiac output or exclude structural heart disease.

Sinus bradycardia has sinus features at a rate below sixty beats per minute. A slower rate increases the time between beats, but its effect on output depends on stroke volume and the person's needs. It may occur normally during sleep or in well-conditioned people, or accompany medications and disease. Do not infer harm, safety, or a treatment choice from the rate label alone. First describe the rhythm and its measured features.

Sinus tachycardia has sinus features at a rate above one hundred beats per minute. It may be an appropriate response to activity or stress, or accompany an underlying problem. At faster rates, diastole shortens and P waves can merge with preceding T waves. The source's usual ceiling of one hundred sixty is not a universal diagnostic limit. Rhythm identification depends on onset, P-wave features, and context, not a single maximum-rate rule.

In respiratory sinus arrhythmia, sinus timing varies with breathing: heart rate usually increases during inspiration and decreases during expiration. P waves retain sinus features, and conduction to the ventricles remains consistent. This is common in healthy younger people. The changing R to R interval does not by itself indicate an ectopic rhythm. Compare the P waves and the repeating breathing-related pattern before naming the irregularity.

A pause means an expected atrial activation is absent or delayed. Distinguishing sinus arrest from sinoatrial exit block requires attention to timing and the available tracing. A three-second cutoff alone does not reliably name the mechanism or prove that a pause is benign. A pause that is an exact multiple of the baseline P to P interval may support exit block in some patterns, but surface strips can be inconclusive. Describe the pause and any escape activity first.

If verified sinus examples are available, compare them. What stays the same when only the rate changes? What makes respiratory sinus arrhythmia different from a premature atrial beat? Find a pause and identify whether an escape complex follows it. For each answer, give the rate, regularity, P-wave evidence, P R relationship, and Q R S duration before the name. Use only strips actually available in the website.

Wandering atrial pacemaker describes shifting atrial pacemaker sites, with at least three distinct P-wave shapes in one lead and variable P R intervals. The rhythm is irregular, and the rate is usually below one hundred beats per minute. If similar multifocal atrial activity is faster, another label may apply. Do not diagnose wandering pacemaker merely because two P waves look slightly different or because the baseline is noisy.

A premature atrial complex begins early from an atrial site outside the sinus node. Look for an early P wave with a different shape, sometimes hidden in the preceding T wave. It may conduct normally, conduct with aberrancy, or fail to conduct to the ventricles. Therefore, a narrow Q R S is common but not required for every atrial premature beat. Identify both the underlying rhythm and the premature atrial event.

Atrial tachycardia originates in atrial tissue rather than the sinus node. In a focal form, organized atrial impulses repeat rapidly, and P-wave shape differs from sinus activation. The ventricular rate depends on how many impulses conduct through the A V node. Rates overlap with other supraventricular tachycardias, so neither a rate range nor a narrow Q R S alone proves the exact mechanism. Analyze atrial activity whenever it can be seen.

Typical atrial flutter is usually a large re-entry circuit in the right atrium, not simply one irritable focus firing repeatedly. Flutter waves may create a sawtooth appearance, especially in certain leads. Atrial rates are often near three hundred per minute, but vary. The A V node usually conducts only some impulses, producing ratios such as two to one. A fixed ratio can make the ventricular rhythm regular; changing conduction can make it irregular.

Atrial fibrillation has disorganized atrial activation without consistent discrete P waves. The ventricular rhythm is typically irregularly irregular when conduction is through the A V node. Exceptions, including pacing or complete block, can change that appearance. Atrial contraction becomes less effective, and blood stasis can increase thromboembolic risk. Do not estimate a precise atrial rate by counting chaotic baseline ripples. Describe the ventricular rate and irregularity separately.

Compare organized repeating flutter waves with the absence of consistent P waves in atrial fibrillation. A regular ventricular rhythm does not exclude flutter, and an irregular one does not prove fibrillation. Look at the atrial activity and conduction pattern. Both rhythms can affect filling and are associated with thromboembolic risk, but a study strip does not determine an individual's risk or treatment. The goal here is recognition and precise description.

For each atrial example, ask three questions. Are there distinct P waves, and how many shapes can you identify? Is an event premature, or is the whole rhythm sustained? Is atrial activity organized, like flutter, or disorganized, like fibrillation? Then calculate the ventricular rate and examine conduction. If artifact obscures the answer, record uncertainty instead of assigning a rhythm from rate alone.

A junctional rhythm begins in or near the A V junction. Activation may travel normally toward the ventricles and backward toward the atria. Retrograde P waves may be inverted in inferior leads, appear before or after the Q R S, or be hidden within it. If a retrograde P wave precedes the Q R S, the P R interval is often short. Surface timing alone does not precisely locate the focus within an upper, middle, or lower node.

A premature junctional complex is an early beat arising from the A V junction. Its Q R S is usually narrow if ventricular conduction is normal. A retrograde P wave may be visible before or after the complex, or may be hidden. Compare the beat with the expected timing of the underlying rhythm. Prematurity distinguishes it from a junctional escape beat, which arrives late after a pause or slowing of higher pacemakers.

A junctional escape rhythm is usually taught at forty to sixty beats per minute. An accelerated junctional rhythm is around sixty to one hundred, and junctional tachycardia is faster than one hundred. Boundaries vary among references. These names combine origin and rate; they do not by themselves describe the person's circulation. Atrial and ventricular timing can vary, and a one-to-one atrial-ventricular relationship is not guaranteed in every junctional rhythm.

Supraventricular tachycardia is a broad category of tachycardias involving tissue above the ventricles, including several different mechanisms. In bedside shorthand, S V T often means a regular narrow-complex tachycardia whose exact mechanism is not yet clear. That shorthand is not the entire formal definition. Some supraventricular rhythms can be irregular, and aberrant conduction can make them wide. Describe the rhythm before assuming a specific mechanism.

Rates overlap among sinus tachycardia, atrial tachycardia, flutter with conduction, and re-entry tachycardias. Hidden P waves make identification harder. Compare regularity, atrial activity, Q R S shape, and any documented onset or termination. This lesson deliberately does not reproduce the audiobook's medication dose or cardioversion sequence. Those are clinical actions requiring current protocols, trained judgment, and information that a website strip alone cannot supply.

Atrioventricular block means delayed or failed conduction from atria to ventricles. The problem can occur in the A V node or farther down in the His-Purkinje system. Track atrial and ventricular activity separately. Count P waves as well as Q R S complexes, and compare their timing. The phrase heart block does not mean that a coronary artery is blocked, and it does not tell us the anatomical level by itself.

First-degree A V block is prolonged atrioventricular conduction: the P R interval is longer than zero point two zero seconds in adults, and every atrial impulse still conducts. It is a delay rather than an intermittent dropped beat. Identify the underlying rhythm, for example sinus rhythm with first-degree A V block. Q R S duration may be narrow or wide depending on other conduction findings. A prolonged P R does not automatically establish normal cardiac output.

In the classic Mobitz one pattern, P R intervals progressively lengthen until a P wave is not followed by a Q R S complex. The sequence then repeats. This creates grouped beating and is often called Wenckebach. The block is commonly within the A V node, but exceptions exist. A narrow Q R S is common, not mandatory. Verify the pattern across enough beats instead of labeling any irregular rhythm with a dropped complex as Wenckebach.

In Mobitz two, an occasional P wave fails to conduct despite a stable sinus rate, with unchanged P R intervals before and after the nonconducted P wave. It reflects conduction failure in the His-Purkinje system, and Q R S complexes are often wide, though they can be narrow. A two-to-one pattern alone cannot distinguish Mobitz one from Mobitz two, because there are not consecutive conducted beats to show progressive P R change. Describe it as two-to-one A V block unless additional evidence resolves the type.

In complete, or third-degree, A V block, atrial impulses do not conduct to the ventricles. When an escape rhythm is present, atrial and ventricular activation proceed independently. An escape rhythm may be slow, unreliable, or absent. P to P and R to R intervals may each be regular, but there is no consistent P R relationship. The escape rate and Q R S width depend on the focus and conduction system. A V dissociation alone is not always proof of complete block; the full pattern matters.

Compare four patterns. A long constant P R with every P conducted suggests first-degree delay. Progressive P R lengthening followed by a nonconducted P suggests Mobitz one. Sudden nonconducted P waves with constant conducted P R intervals suggest Mobitz two when the pattern supports that diagnosis. Independent atrial and ventricular rhythms raise concern for complete block. Give the evidence, acknowledge limitations, and follow the course's escalation expectations rather than selecting a treatment in this lesson.

An artificial pacemaker senses cardiac electrical activity and can deliver timed electrical stimuli. The pulse generator contains the power source and circuitry. Leads connect it to electrodes in or on the heart, although leadless systems also exist. A pacing stimulus may appear as a narrow spike on the E C G, but modern spikes are not always easily visible. The device supports electrical timing; an electrical response still does not by itself prove an effective mechanical pulse.

Transcutaneous pacing delivers stimuli through skin pads and is generally temporary. Temporary transvenous pacing uses a lead passed through a vein. Implanted systems provide longer-term support, with configurations chosen for the clinical problem. This module identifies devices and recording patterns only. It does not specify pad placement, current settings, thresholds, or programming steps. Those require equipment-specific training, current protocols, and clinical supervision.

Pacing rate, output, and sensing are different settings. Sensing determines how the device detects intrinsic activity. Output relates to the delivered stimulus. In an inhibited demand mode, a sensed event can prevent an unnecessary pacing pulse. In an asynchronous mode, stimuli occur without responding to intrinsic events in the usual way. Triggered and dual-chamber behaviors follow particular timing rules; they are not simply a response to any missed or abnormal beat.

Atrial pacing may show a stimulus followed by a P wave if atrial capture occurs. Ventricular pacing may show a stimulus followed by a paced Q R S, often wider with conventional ventricular pacing. Dual-chamber systems can sense and pace both chambers, but a strip does not always show two spikes on every cycle. Atrial-only pacing requires appropriate atrial tissue and atrioventricular conduction; it is not a standard solution for permanent atrial fibrillation.

Cardiac resynchronization therapy coordinates ventricular activation in selected patients with ventricular dyssynchrony. Traditional biventricular systems stimulate right and left ventricular regions. The visible number or spacing of spikes alone does not establish correct resynchronization. Some newer pacing strategies activate the conduction system more directly. Device selection and programming are clinical decisions, while this study module focuses on recognizing the limits of what the surface recording can show.

Electrical failure to capture means a pacing stimulus is not followed by the expected atrial or ventricular depolarization. Undersensing may produce stimuli despite intrinsic events; oversensing may inhibit needed pacing. Apparent failure to output requires context, including the programmed mode and rate, because the absence of a visible pacing spike does not necessarily indicate malfunction. Mechanical capture is a separate assessment. Do not diagnose device failure or change settings from spike position alone.

Connect the anatomy to vocabulary. Stenosis is narrowing that obstructs forward flow. Regurgitation is backward leakage. Atresia is an absent or closed normal opening. Cardiomyopathy affects heart muscle. Heart failure is a clinical syndrome caused by impaired cardiac filling or pumping, which can produce congestion, inadequate circulation, or both. It can occur with reduced or preserved ejection fraction; a normal ejection fraction alone does not diagnose a filling problem or exclude heart failure.

Pericarditis affects the sac around the heart. Myocarditis affects the heart muscle. Endocarditis often involves infection of the endocardial surface, especially valves, although noninfectious forms exist. Ischemia means inadequate blood supply relative to tissue needs; infarction means tissue death caused by prolonged inadequate supply. Adult heart muscle has limited regenerative capacity, and significant injury often leaves scar. Avoid the absolute claim that no cardiac cell can ever renew.

Atherosclerosis is a complex inflammatory plaque process involving lipids, cells, fibrous tissue, and sometimes calcium in artery walls. Plaque can narrow a vessel; disruption can trigger local clot formation and acute loss of flow. Arteriosclerosis is the broader term for arterial thickening and stiffening. H D L and L D L are lipoproteins, not simply good and bad fats. Tissue injury depends on blood supply, demand, duration, and collateral flow, not a claim that everything below one clot immediately dies.

Sympathetic activity generally increases heart rate, conduction, and contractile force. Parasympathetic activity through the vagus mainly slows sinus rate and A V nodal conduction. Vascular responses depend on receptor type and tissue; sympathetic activity does not simply dilate every vessel, and parasympathetic activity does not universally constrict them. Hormones also affect circulation: vasopressin promotes water retention, aldosterone promotes sodium retention, and atrial natriuretic peptide promotes sodium and water excretion.

Some medicines change heart rate, conduction, ion currents, or contractile force. Examples include beta blockers, selected calcium-channel blockers, antiarrhythmic drugs, and digoxin. Their effects differ by drug and tissue, so a class label is not a complete prediction of a tracing. Digoxin inhibits the sodium-potassium pump, indirectly affecting calcium handling. This is mechanism vocabulary for study, not guidance to start, stop, select, or dose a medication.

E C G and E K G name the same type of recording. The electrocardiograph is the instrument; the electrocardiogram is the recording. Augustus Waller published a human electrocardiogram in eighteen eighty-seven. Willem Einthoven developed the string-galvanometer method in the early nineteen hundreds and received the nineteen twenty-four Nobel Prize. Monitoring work requires careful observation, communication, and facility-specific training. Workload, pay, shifts, and certification requirements vary, so the source's examples are not universal facts.

Finish by connecting the levels. Trace blood through four chambers and four valves. Trace the impulse through S A node, A V node, His bundle, branches, and Purkinje fibers on the same heart. Explain how calcium permits sarcomere force and how its removal permits relaxation. Follow air to the alveolus and oxygen into pulmonary blood. When a verified practice strip is available, apply the six-step method to it. When evidence is missing, name the uncertainty instead of guessing.

Heart-disease risk reflects both nonmodifiable factors, such as age and inherited background, and modifiable factors, such as smoking, blood pressure, cholesterol, and activity patterns. Conditions can have overlapping symptoms, including breathlessness, fatigue, swelling, palpitations, or chest discomfort. A symptom list does not identify one disease or prove that a rhythm is its cause. In this lesson, connect the vocabulary to anatomy and function without making a diagnosis from a model, a strip, or a checklist.
